Updated assessment incorporating the July 2021 Beige Book and SLOOS:

- Policy stance: Holding the funds rate at 0–1/4 percent and continuing $80B Treasuries/$40B MBS purchases remains appropriate. The Beige Book reports continued strengthening in activity and employment, with pandemic-affected sectors improving but not fully recovered—consistent with maintaining an accommodative stance until maximum employment is achieved and inflation moderately exceeds 2 percent for some time.

- Real-side conditions (Beige Book cross-check): District reports highlight increases in hiring and wages, and a rebound in tourism—particularly notable in the New York area. These developments corroborate ongoing labor market healing and improving demand in services most impacted by the pandemic.

- Credit supply and demand (SLOOS cross-check): Banks report stronger C&I loan demand across firm sizes, easing C&I terms, broader easing for consumer credit (credit cards, autos, other), and firmer demand in several residential mortgage categories; multifamily CRE standards eased. These findings support the FOMC’s view that financial conditions are accommodative and that the flow of credit to households and businesses is improving.

- Growth/inflation balance: The Beige Book’s stronger hiring and tourism, alongside SLOOS-reported credit easing, point to a firmer near-term growth impulse. At the same time, widespread wage increases suggest some risk that inflation could prove more persistent than purely transitory factors, warranting vigilance even as expectations remain well anchored.

- Risks: Virus dynamics still matter for the outlook. Financial stability vulnerabilities flagged elsewhere (elevated valuations, leverage, nonbank fragilities) persist, but the absence of tightening in bank lending standards lowers near-term downside risks from credit supply constraints.

Bottom line: Cautiously more constructive on growth and employment than previously, given Beige Book evidence of rising hiring, wages, and tourism alongside SLOOS-confirmed credit transmission. Inflation risks tilt slightly higher due to wage pressures but remain manageable under current policy communication.
